prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged from round 1: a single part for the optical lattice clock, credited to Katori and Ye. The reason I hold it is the mechanism. Choosing a magic wavelength cancels the differential light shift of the lattice, so many atoms can be held in the Lamb-Dicke regime and interrogated together without Doppler or recoil broadening. The statistical gain from many atoms and the removal of the dominant systematic come from the same one idea, and that is the kind of simple, general mechanism that explains why the clock works and not only that it works. It is reproduced independently in several laboratories and species at the 10^-18 level, and it has produced results that are physics and not only metrology: gravitational redshift resolved over millimetres, bounds on drifting constants and ultralight dark matter, and many-body (spin-exchange and interaction) effects that had to be understood to reach the accuracy. After the chair's questions I would keep the citation narrow and tied to the lattice clock, with the 10^-18 level as the measurable consequence, and I would not add a second part. A second part would need either five names or a candidate whose credit I could defend in one or two names, and I cannot find one among the alternatives.
statement.case_against: The distinctness question is real, and I treat it as a judgement and not a settled fact. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a frequency ruler and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems, so a sceptic can read the lattice clock as the next step in a lineage the Academy has already honoured twice. My answer is that the lattice clock rests on a different physical idea, the magic-wavelength condition applied to many neutral atoms, which follows from neither of the earlier prizes, but a colleague who weights instrument advances more strictly could still disagree. The attribution is also a simplification: Lemonde, Takamoto, Ludlow, Boyd, Hollberg and the Yb, Hg and ion-clock groups made real contributions that a limit of three names cannot all carry. Finally, all eight of us are working from recalled chronology, so the priority statement that Katori proposed the magic wavelength and realised the first strontium lattice clock, while Ye's group set the accuracy records, has not been checked against the primary 2003 to 2005 papers in this room.

responses.point: Danielsson says he gave up his EHT first choice for the clock because a prize has to be buildable around a discovery, and he lists the pending redefinition of the second and the exact Katori-Ye weighting as open.
responses.response: I agree with the trade you describe, and I share the hesitation about timing, but I now come down on not waiting. The redefinition of the second is a consequence of the clocks, not a condition for their scientific case: the accuracy, the independent reproduction and the redshift measurements already exist. Waiting also lets the field grow around the credit, which is the opposite of what a two-name prize needs. On the weighting I would not rank the two names. Katori's idea makes the device possible and Ye's work establishes what it can do, and I would drop neither.

responses.point: Olsson says the prize is not for the second discoverer who did it better, tests the clock against that charge, and asks that the record be checked against the 2003 to 2005 papers for priority.
responses.response: That is the right test, and I think the clock passes it for a specific reason: the magic-wavelength condition is a new idea that does not follow from the comb or from ion traps. I support your request for a primary-source check, with a caveat. Priority for the concept is Katori's by the record we all recall, so a check could change the wording of the citation but I do not expect it to change the names. If the paper trail showed that another group had the magic-wavelength idea first, that would be a reason to reopen the credit, and I would want the chair to say so before the ballot rather than after it.

responses.point: Pearce keeps IceCube (B033) and the EHT (B052) as alternatives, relies on the atomic-physics members for the clock chronology, and asks whether a second part is needed.
responses.response: I respect the detector work behind B033, and I would use it as my own second alternative, but I hold the earlier concern: the origin of the diffuse flux is unresolved and the point-source evidence is modest, so the case is less complete than the clock. On a second part, I do not think it is needed. Adding IceCube would raise the credit to four names with the two clock laureates, which breaks the three-name limit, and I would rather give one prize whose credit I trust than a pair in which one part is weaker. Your reliance on Lindroth, Kroll and Johansson for the chronology is sensible, and I rely on them in the same way.

responses.point: Kroll says the redefinition of the second should not by itself be a reason to wait and adds that waiting risks a missed or contested attribution as the field grows; he also declines B025 as a second part.
responses.response: I agree with both points. The contested-attribution risk is the strongest argument against delay, since each year more groups reach 10^-18 and the Lemonde and Takamoto claims become harder to separate from the general clock community. I also agree that B025 does not work as a second part here: the credit there needs a decision about Chu and about Bordé that the clock does not. On the citation wording you favour, a phrase about opening a new regime of precision, I prefer naming the lattice clock and the 10^-18 level, because that wording does more to answer the objection about the 2005 and 2012 prizes.

responses.point: Eriksson moved from topological insulators to the clock, and says a weak attribution is a worse flaw than a modest novelty question, noting that B019 omits Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu and Moore.
responses.response: I agree, and it is the same reason I keep B019 only as an alternative. The physics is deeper there, but a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp slate has to be defended against the HgTe proposal and the three-dimensional work, and the 2016 prize overlaps. The clock has a fixed two-name credit and no overlap of that kind. I would add one point to your comparison of novelty: the instrument-versus-discovery objection applies less here than for most metrology, because the many-body clock physics that had to be understood to reach 10^-18 is physics in its own right.

uncertainties: Whether the full committee accepts the lattice clock as distinct from the 2005 comb and 2012 ion-control prizes; I judge it distinct, but this is a judgement.

Whether the 2003 to 2005 primary papers support Katori's priority for the magic-wavelength proposal and the first strontium lattice clocks, and whether Lemonde, Takamoto or others would displace or join Katori and Ye; I rely on recalled chronology.
Whether the pending SI redefinition of the second should affect timing; I now say it should not, but I accept that others hold it as open.
Whether B019 or B033 could be given a credit set that I could defend; at present I cannot, and I regard both as alternatives, not as parts.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the preferred configuration. I share a Gothenburg physics environment with Johansson and Olsson (Chalmers) but have no known collaboration with Katori, Ye or any name credited in the alternatives. I note the disclosures of Johansson (B001), Eriksson (2025 chair), Kroll (Boulder) and Olsson (Tokyo); none touches the B048-only configuration in a way that I think requires recusal. My earlier KPZ ranking reflected my own field of statistical physics, and I have withdrawn it for this year.
